paras: The West Liberty ball-ground riot was a clash on May 31, 1903, at the High Bridge baseball ground in West Liberty borough, adjoining Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, in which a white crowd pursued Black men described as gamblers, killed Charles Kelly and dragged William Davis to a tree with a rope on his neck. Sandy Garrett, a Black man who had ordered the gamblers away, died of his wound three days later. Wire reports called it a lynching narrowly averted, Southern editors counted it a Northern lynching, and the Cleveland Gazette denied it was a race riot.

About 2,000 people had come to watch two local amateur teams. According to the New York Sun, the Beltzhoover club could play on Sunday only if it kept gamblers away. When five or six Black men began shooting craps nearby, Garrett, called the club's mascot in the main wire account and "a negro constable" in the Sun, ordered them off with players behind him.
The gamblers refused and, by the wire account, drew revolvers and fired. Some 1,000 men and boys gave chase, and Nelson (or George) Foster was caught, beaten and thrown over a hill.

Kelly and Davis fired from a chicken coop, and Garrett was shot in the chest when he rushed it. The Sun said the two surrendered with a handkerchief once their ammunition ran out and that Kelly was shot through the heart as he came out. The longer wire account said a man on the roof dropped a rock on Kelly's head and the crowd then beat him to death.

The crowd put a rope on Davis's neck and dragged him about 300 yards to a tree, beating him on the way. As men climbed to fasten the rope, someone shouted, "Let him alone, let the law deal with him," another called that officers were coming, and the crowd left Davis on the ground. The Sun credited former Police Inspector George Waggoner and the Pittsburg police, and the Selma Times "a pitying prize fighter." Three white youths were reported shot by the gamblers.

On June 1 county authorities began investigating what a Pittsburg dispatch called "the race riot and murder at West Liberty." Police were arresting "suspicious negroes," and County Detective Robinson had the names of eight alleged leaders to be charged with murder. Garrett died on the night of June 3; a post-mortem found a bullet through his lung and heart, with gangrene the direct cause.

Davis was well enough by then to be sent from the hospital to the county jail by Coroner McGeary. Thirty-three riot warrants had been sworn out and four arrests made, among them the pugilist Louden Campbell, and Attorney Haymaker said no guilty man, "white or black," would go unpunished. No report of an inquest verdict, indictment or trial was found.

On June 1 the Sun's "Race Rioting at Pittsburg" reappeared in the Washington Times with a subhead calling Davis a "Desperado." A longer wire account ran as "Lynching Narrowly Averted" in the Daily Morning Journal and Courier and "Guns, Clubs, Rocks Used upon Black Gamblers" in the Wheeling Register. Shorter items from Utah to Alabama used headlines such as "A Game of Craps," and a variant dispatch counted "two negroes and a white boy" killed.

Southern papers turned it against the North: the Selma Times, reprinted by the Montgomery Advertiser as "Our Blind Neighbors," and the Brunswick Daily News stressed that it happened in Pennsylvania. The Savannah Morning News counted it among Northern lynchings, and The Commonwealth wrote of men "hanged and beaten to death with base ball bats" there, though no hanging was reported.

The only contemporary Black-press item found, a June 13 Cleveland Gazette editorial paragraph, called it no race riot but a fight between two mixed crowds that left one white and one colored man dead. It blamed "the Associated Press liar" for the national reports.

Death counts ranged from one Black man to "two negroes and a white boy," but no report named a white person who died. In January 1904 an Atlanta Independent column said "the Pittsburg riot" began when a white man was caught with a colored woman, a version that gives no date and matches no 1903 report.

reader.title: West Liberty ball-ground riot
bases: A white crowd pursuing armed Black gamblers killed Charles Kelly after he was disarmed or had surrendered and dragged William Davis to a tree with a rope on his neck before abandoning the hanging (A1, A4, A5).

Kelly was killed by a crowd of hundreds, shot after surrendering (A1) or knocked down with a rock and 'pounded to death' (A4), and the same crowd roped Davis to hang him until someone urged them to 'let the law deal with him' (A4, A5); but the killing came out of an armed exchange in which the Black men had shot Garrett and white youths, and the Cleveland Gazette called it a fight between mixed crowds (A33), so it is not clearly punishment under a pretext of justice.

Two independent wire versions (A1; A4, A11) and later Pittsburg dispatches (A18, A25, A28) agree on the riot, Kelly's death and the near-hanging of Davis, though the Cleveland Gazette disputes its racial character (A33).

accounts.label: Sun wire
accounts.gist: Five gamblers outside the grounds refused Constable Garrett's order and shot a white boy; Kelly and Davis held out in a coop until they surrendered with a handkerchief, then Kelly was shot dead and Davis dragged with bats to a tree until Waggoner pleaded and police came.

accounts.label: Associated wire (long)
accounts.gist: Six crap shooters drew revolvers on the club mascot Garrett and players; 1,000 pursued; a rock dropped from the coop roof felled Kelley, who was pounded to death; Davis was roped and dragged 300 yards until someone urged the crowd to let the law deal with him.

accounts.label: Variant dispatch
accounts.gist: Two negroes and a white boy were killed and a third negro was rescued from lynching by officers.

accounts.label: Pittsburg follow-ups
accounts.gist: County authorities investigated a 'race riot and murder', arrested suspects on both sides, swore out 33 riot warrants; Garrett died of his wound and Davis was jailed.

accounts.label: Black editor
accounts.gist: The Cleveland Gazette said it was not a race riot but a fight between two mixed crowds, leaving one white and one colored dead, and that the Associated Press had lied.

accounts.label: Later Black columnist
accounts.gist: An Atlanta Independent column said 'the Pittsburg riot' arose over a white man caught with a colored woman; its link to this event is uncertain.

framing.detail: Headlines stressed gambling and the near-lynching: 'Fatal Riot at Ball Game / Lynching Narrowly Averted', 'Guns, Clubs, Rocks Used upon Black Gamblers', 'Mascot Didn't Like the Crap Shooters'.
The Sun version, headlined 'Race Rioting at Pittsburg', ran in the Washington Times as 'Pittsburgers Attempt to Lynch a Negro / Desperado Dragged and Beaten'.

Southern editorials used the event to charge Northern hypocrisy about lynching ('Our Blind Neighbors'; a negro 'beaten to death at Pittsburg'), while The Commonwealth called the victims 'murdered negroes'.
The Cleveland Gazette rejected the 'race riot' label and blamed 'the Associated Press liar' for the national coverage.
